[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The query is a triptan (3-(2-dimethylaminoethyl)indole with a 5-(pyrrolidin-1-ylsulfonylmethyl) substituent); L6 retrieves hepatic-clearance records for close triptan analogs rizatriptan and eletriptan.

Rizatriptan, a close triptan analog, has moderate human liver microsomal intrinsic clearance (~11–12 µL/min/mg) that is MAO-mediated (pargyline-sensitive, minimal NADPH effect), not an extreme first-pass clearance.
Eletriptan, a triptan with a sulfonyl-containing 5-substituent, has low-to-moderate HLM intrinsic clearance (3.02–4.34 µL/min/mg) and CYP-mediated metabolism without MAO involvement.

5-MeO-DMT, a less transferable tryptamine lacking the 5-sulfonylmethyl substituent, shows high hepatocyte intrinsic clearance (81.9–92.1 µL/min/10^6 cells), but this does not transfer to the query because of the different 5-substituent and metabolic context.

L1 gold contexts are predominantly high absolute F measurements (bepridil 59–62%, vilazodone 72%, flavoxate ~100%, sulthiame complete, 5-HTP 49%); the only low-F context (ilomastat) is structurally unrelated.

L3/L4/L5 records for triptans and basic amines show measurable oral systemic exposure, high aqueous solubility across GI pH, high absorptive Caco-2/intestinal permeability, and only modest non-saturating efflux.
No transferable threshold-relevant evidence supports F < 20% for the query; unresolved uncertainty is expressed through confidence and gaps, not as a low prediction.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for almotriptan is present in any card.
No matched oral-versus-IV AUC/Cmax comparison is available for the query.
No query-specific hepatic clearance or metabolic stability measurement exists; L6 values come from analogs (rizatriptan, eletriptan, 5-MeO-DMT, imipramine, etc.).
L6 records are mechanistic and not direct F endpoints; species/assay differences (HLM, hepatocytes, rat/mouse) limit quantitative transfer.
High-clearance 5-MeO-DMT records (C201, C209) have low transferability due to the different 5-substituent and metabolic context.
Food effect and formulation dependence for the query are unknown.

L1 gold contexts are predominantly high absolute F; L3-L5 show oral exposure, high solubility, and high absorptive permeability for close triptan analogs and basic amines; L6 adds hepatic-clearance records showing moderate, not extreme, HLM intrinsic clearance for rizatriptan and eletriptan, reducing first-pass concern. High-clearance 5-MeO-DMT records are not transferable due to structural differences. No threshold-relevant low-F evidence transfers to the query; confidence remains moderate because no direct query-specific F measurement exists.

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
